title: The living flame
hook: John's poem of love like a flame that wounds gently

segments.voice: Yesterday, nada: John of the Cross and the narrow path of nothing up the mountain. Your line was nothing, for all. What did you loosen your grip on? Day one thousand one hundred thirty-seven.

Same friar, a different voice. Yesterday John of the Cross was drawing a steep mountain with nothing written up its side. Today he's writing a love poem. It opens with a cry, which in English runs something like this: O living flame of love, that tenderly wounds my soul in its deepest center. Wounds, and tenderly, in the same breath. That's not how burns usually go. The man who taught letting go of everything also wrote lines this warm, and wrote them about God. For John, the two belong together. Today's word is the poem's opening image. The living flame.

John wrote the poem, and then, because a friend asked, a long commentary explaining it line by line. The flame, he says, is the Holy Spirit. That's an old image in the Bible. At Pentecost, the book of Acts says, "there appeared unto them cloven tongues like as of fire, and it sat upon each of them." And the Song of Songs says love's coals "are coals of fire, which hath a most vehement flame." So why would a loving flame wound? John uses a picture from the hearth. Put a damp log on a fire. At first the fire doesn't look friendly. The log hisses, blackens, smokes, and lets out all the water it was holding. That's the hard part, the purifying. But the fire is the same fire the whole time. It isn't angry at the log. It's turning the log into itself. In the end, the wood glows, and you can't tell where the log stops and the flame begins. For John, that's what God's love does to a person. The pain of being changed and the joy of being loved are one fire, felt at different stages. That's why, for John, the wound is tender: love that hurts only because it's getting in. And notice where the flame reaches in the poem: the deepest center. The same center Teresa put the King in, two days ago. The two friends seem to be pointing at the same room. One built a castle around it. The other set it on fire.
screen: `ONE FIRE: THE HURT AND THE LOVE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: watch a flame. If you can do it safely, strike a match or light a candle, and just watch. If you can't, call one to mind, or look at a picture of one. See how it moves and doesn't stay still. See where it's blue and where it's gold. Notice that it turns whatever it touches into more of itself. If you pray, you can let the flame stand for the Holy Spirit, as John did. If you don't, just watch the light. Blow out any real flame before the end. The bell holds the time.
The living flame. John of the Cross's image of the Holy Spirit's love: a fire that wounds gently, burns away what's damp, and turns the soul into flame.
Your line: o living flame. Today, when something stings because it's changing you, ask whether it's a fire that destroys or one that's making the log glow. Day one thousand one hundred thirty-seven.

howItsDone: Carmelites and other readers of John of the Cross pray with his poems slowly, sometimes aloud, and his Living Flame of Love is read in retreats on the work of the Holy Spirit.

fork.setup: you're a damp log on John's fire. you hiss, you smoke, you blacken. what's happening, in his picture?
options: the same loving fire is turning you into itself.
fork.reveal: John says the fire is one fire from start to finish. the hard part is the log letting go of its damp; the end is wood that glows.

trapdoor: what you thought: a flame is something that burns you.
what it means: John's picture of the Holy Spirit's love, which wounds gently and turns the soul into fire.
what a scholar hears: in his commentary on the Living Flame, John explains the hurt with a log in a fire: the same fire first dries and blackens, then makes the wood glow.

notes: The opening line ('¡Oh llama de amor viva, que tiernamente hieres de mi alma en el más profundo centro!') is paraphrased, not quoted; confirm the English sense.
'Because friends asked' paraphrases the dedication of the commentary to Doña Ana de Peñalosa; confirm or soften to 'at a friend's request'.
The log-in-the-fire image appears in the Living Flame commentary (stanza 1) and the Dark Night (II.10); confirm the attribution to the Living Flame commentary.
'The flame, he says, is the Holy Spirit' follows John's commentary on stanza 1; confirm.
'Which John loved' (the Song of Songs) rests on his Spiritual Canticle being modeled on it; confirm or cut.
